common_name: Flordagrand Blackberry (Low-Chill Central Florida Trailing Bramble)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in winter (December-February) in Central Florida and along the Gulf Coast, spacing plants 6-8 feet apart in rows and providing a trellis, since the long canes trail rather than stand upright.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, sandy soil and train the long, thorny, trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis, since this cultivar sprawls rather than growing upright on its own. Flordagrand was released by the University of Florida in the 1950s specifically for the low-chill conditions of Central Florida and the Gulf Coast, where its evergreen canes need only a fraction of the winter chilling hours that Northern blackberries require. The berries are large and flavorful, ripening in April and May, but the plant is largely self-unfruitful and must be interplanted with its University of Florida companion release 'Oklawaha' to set a full crop. Because of its sprawling, thorny canes it never became a commercial crop, but it remains a dependable heirloom choice for gardeners in the Deep South who need a blackberry that thrives with minimal winter cold.

common_name: Oklawaha Blackberry (Low-Chill Central Florida Trailing Bramble)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in winter (December-February) in Central Florida and along the Gulf Coast, spacing plants 6-8 feet apart in rows and providing a trellis, since the long canes trail rather than stand upright.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, sandy soil and train the long, thorny, trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis, since they will not stand upright on their own. Oklawaha was released by the University of Florida alongside 'Flordagrand' in the 1950s, bred specifically to serve as its cross-pollenizer, since both cultivars are largely self-unfruitful and set their best crops when planted in alternating rows together. Like its companion, Oklawaha needs only a low number of winter chilling hours, stays evergreen through mild Central Florida and Gulf Coast winters, and produces large, attractive berries that ripen in April and May. It remains valued by Deep South gardeners as the traditional pollenizer partner for Flordagrand in low-chill home plantings.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 6-8 feet apart in rows at least 8-10 feet apart, and install a sturdy two- or three-wire trellis at planting time since the canes trail and will not support themselves.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil and train the long, thornless trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis, since like other trailing types they will not support themselves. Waldo was released by the USDA-ARS breeding program in Oregon in 1989 as the first thornless trailing blackberry ever introduced, a milestone that made hand-harvesting far safer than with the thorny trailing types that preceded it. The berries are medium-sized with a notably high drupelet count, ripening late in the trailing-blackberry season, and the canes show good resistance to common foliar diseases. Waldo's flavor is considered milder and less aromatic than the thorny standard 'Marion', so it has mainly been used as a parent in later thornless breeding programs rather than planted widely on its own.

common_name: Obsidian Blackberry (Thornless Trailing Bramble with Marion-Like Flavor)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 6-8 feet apart in rows at least 8-10 feet apart, and install a sturdy trellis at planting time to support the vigorous, sprawling canes.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil and train the vigorous, thornless trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis, since the sprawling growth habit needs support to keep fruiting laterals off the ground. Obsidian was released in 2005 by the USDA-ARS breeding program working with Oregon State University, bred from Marion, Olallie, and Boysen parentage to combine thornless canes with fruit quality much closer to the industry-standard 'Marion' than earlier thornless trailing types like 'Waldo'. The berries are large, glossy black, firm, and richly flavored, ripening early in the trailing-blackberry season around mid-to-late June. Its combination of thornless canes and excellent dessert and processing quality has made Obsidian one of the more widely planted modern replacements for thorny Marion.
